newsitem.title: MEXICO: INSTANT VIEW-Mexico inflation, retail data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Mexico inflation, retail data.

text.p: Mexican inflation data released Friday came as little surprise to analysts, who said the 0.89 percent CPI figure for the first half of November was in line with expectations.
Retail and wholesale sales data also released Friday did contain surprises for some, however.
Retail sales were down 1.8 percent in September versus the same month a year ago, while September wholesale sales rose 3.1 percent over the same period.

The wholesale figures were in line with expectations but a Reuters survey of 11 brokerages, banks and research firms had forecast a rise of 0.99 percent in retail sales over the same period a year ago.

The inflation figure "was marginally higher than expected but there is room for the second half of the month to be lower," said Ann Ginsberg of brokerage Valores Finamex. "We are looking at around 1.6 percent for the month...it's within expectations."
Chip Brown of Morgan Stanley was unexcited by the inflation data.
"I think the inflation number is a non-event," he said. "It's right in there, you always get more in the first half of the month. This number pretty much meets our expectations for the month."
Brown said though that the retail and wholesale data suggested that "the Mexican consumer is not in the recovery yet".
"The wholesale number clearly shows the start of a seasonal trend, that is, Christmas buying," Brown said.

"The retail number underscores one of the concerns I have been expressing, which is: where is the Mexican consumer in this recovery? He's being pinched in wages and in hours worked...and he's not in it."

In the aftermath of the December 1994 peso crash, Mexicans went into the consumer equivalent of a coma as more than a million people lost their jobs and soaring interest rates threw millions more into debt.
The only bright spot for the last two years has been the export sector, bolstered by a cheap peso, that has steadily dragged the economy back from the brink of collapse.

Third quarter GDP data released Thursday suggested to some economists that Mexicans were finally beginning to spend again. The economy grew 7.4 percent compared with the third quarter of 1995, and the service sector grew 5.4 percent.
The retail sales figure continued the lackluster form seen throughout 1996, though, dampening a little the optimism generated by the GDP figures.
Gerardo Copca of Valores Finamex said he did not expect to see data showing a pick-up in domestic demand until December.
Brown said he expected increases of only about three percent in domestic demand this year and next.
"I think it's going to be a gradual process, it's going to be next year's news," he said.
Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz has said though that the Mexican economy will grow by at least three percent this year and four percent next year on only a modest increase in domestic demand.
